query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a high‐temperature, dense CrN coating via reactive sputtering onto the surface of boride-based components will act as an effective barrier, thereby improving resistance to molten‐aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment that are prone to corrosion when exposed to molten aluminum.
generation.intervention: Apply a high-temperature, dense CrN coating via reactive sputtering.
generation.conditions: The components are exposed to molten aluminum under typical hot-dip plating process temperatures. The coating is expected to be intact and adherent under prolonged high-temperature service.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense and stable CrN film deposited on the surface.
generation.mechanism: The CrN layer acts as a diffusion barrier that prevents or retards the penetration of molten aluminum and limits the corrosive interactions at the boride surface, similar to its proven protective behavior on stainless steels and related alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated components will exhibit a significantly lower corrosion rate (e.g., reduced weight loss, diminished pit formation, and improved surface integrity) in molten aluminum compared to uncoated components.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components without the CrN protective coating.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to hold as long as the CrN film remains intact and is not mechanically compromised or exposed to temperatures well beyond the tested hot-dip plating range. Extreme mechanical wear or unforeseen chemical interactions might limit its protective capabilities.
generation.uncertainty: While reactive-sputtered CrN coatings have proven benefits on similar materials (e.g., stainless steels and medium-entropy alloys), the exact magnitude of corrosion resistance improvement on boride-based components in molten aluminum is uncertain until directly tested.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identically fabricated boride-based components: one set with the reactive-sputtered CrN coating and one uncoated control set. Expose both groups to molten aluminum at representative hot-dip plating temperatures for a fixed period. Ensure identical mechanical and thermal histories. After exposure, evaluate corrosion damage through weight loss measurements, microscopic surface analysis, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.
measurements: Surface morphology and pit density via scanning electron microscopy
Electrochemical impedance measurements to assess barrier properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrN-coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion indicators (e.g., weight loss, pit formation, impedance degradation) compared to the uncoated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In addition, to obtain a uniform and stable protective layer, sputtering technology offers a fast deposition rate and a low-cost solution. Although the development of HEA systems has been going on for more than a decade, there are few reports on the deposition of stable protective films on HEA surfaces by conventional reactive sputtering techniques. Many studies have shown that sputter deposition of CrN film on conventional stainless steel is beneficial for its wear and corrosion resistance [,]. The CrN film deposited on the surface of 316 stainless steel has a positive effect on the friction behavior in NaCl solution and high temperature environments until heated to 550 °C []. In the tribo-corrosion test, the CrN coating layer can also remain relatively stable during the ball-on-plate sliding under various applied potentials []. As stainless steels are similar to CoCrNi-based MEAs in terms of their single FCC structure and lattice constant, this study attempts to sputter CrN film with a Cr buffer layer on the surface of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA and discusses in detail the improvement of corrosion and wear resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA by sputtering CrN film.

reading.lever: Deposit a high-temperature, dense protective CrN coating via reactive sputtering to act as an effective barrier.
reading.why: This approach, proven on stainless steels and MEAs, is a promising, adaptable intervention to mitigate molten-aluminum attack on boride-based components.
